summary:
Sections 153, 154 and 155 of the Penal Code criminalise male homosexual intercourse, attempts to commit it, and gross indecency between males. All three are felonies, carrying maximum sentences of 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively. The provisions date to the colonial period, and ILGA World's jurisdiction database records them as still in force.

The exposure is defined by sex. Because the offences apply to male persons, a transgender woman whom police read as male falls within their scope; what matters at charge or in custody is the classification officers apply, not how she identifies. For a trans visitor who has sex with a man in Tuvalu, the statute creates a felony exposure in principle regardless of how rarely it is used.

The male homosexual provisions also carry heavier penalties than other sexual conduct. The age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal sex and for sex between women, while conduct between men is dealt with under the felony provisions above. A young trans visitor read as male is exposed to those maximums rather than to the age-of-consent regime.

Enforcement evidence is thin and dated. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tuvalu records no prosecutions of consenting adults under these provisions and reports no government abuses of LGBT people that year, attributing discrimination to traditional customs that perpetuate religious and social prejudice rather than to state action. No later enforcement record was identified for this assessment.

No hate-crime legislation is documented for Tuvalu, and no hate-crime incidents or statistics are recorded. Violence or harassment directed at someone because of gender identity or sexual orientation would not meet a specific aggravated offence on the material reviewed.

In 2011 Tuvalu signed the United Nations joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That signature records a diplomatic position and does not amend the Penal Code. No domestic measure implementing it is documented.

Tuvalu recognises neither marriage nor civil union between two people of the same sex. The 2023 constitutional amendments bar recognition of same-sex marriage, and section 43(2)(b) of the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities defines a family unit as a marriage between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others. The Marriage Act (Cap 29) lists no such restriction among its restrictions on marriage and does not expressly prohibit recognition of foreign same-sex unions, but its provisions assume the parties are male and female. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognition route, and the Act contains no provision for recognising a union entered elsewhere.
tangentialFactors:
Tuvalu's Ministry of Health set out the national HIV response in its 2017 Global AIDS Progress Report to UNAIDS, drawing on the Pacific Multi-Country Mapping and Behavioural Study on HIV and STI risk and vulnerability among key populations. That study covers men who have sex with men and transgender Tuvaluans, so the public-health framework names transgender people as a key population even though the criminal law draws no such distinction.

2017 UNAIDS estimates put the population at roughly 300 men who have sex with men and about 40 pinapinaaine. A 2005 study found that about 14% of young Tuvaluan men aged 15 to 24 reported sex with a male partner at some point in their lives.

These figures come from domestic surveillance and prevalence work carried out inside a criminalised environment. They describe the resident population and the shape of the national health response rather than any service open to a visitor, and no trans-specific clinic, referral pathway or health service for visitors is identified.
localsOnly:
The Labour and Employment Relations Act 2017 bans workplace discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation, within a protected list that also covers gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, HIV/AIDS status and disability. Gender identity and gender expression are not named among the grounds as described.

Constitutional protection is narrower. Section 27 of the Constitution, as amended in 2023, lists sex among the attributes protected from discrimination but does not refer to sexual orientation, and no gender-identity or gender-expression protection appears in the sources consulted.
outOfScopeNotes:
No finding on detention conditions, strip searches or the custody treatment of transgender detainees was identified. The custody exposure rests on the statutory maximum alone; no documented case of a transgender person held under these provisions was found.

No partner-visa, next-of-kin or foreign-union recognition provision is addressed anywhere in the sources reviewed.

No education-policy, school-bullying or youth-service findings are available, and no hate-crime incident statistics or enforcement data later than 2013 were identified.
